learning_outcomes.text: The mechanical properties of various materials via the basic engineering test methods.
The basic elements of semiconductor physics and technology (conductivity, carrier type, types of dopants, thermal diffusion doping) and of semiconductor diodes.

The basic aspects and use of high dielectric permittivity materials, fabrication of powders and pellets using liquid chemistry followed by high-temperature calcination, structural characterization by X-Ray diffractometry and dielectric assessment by impedance spectroscopy and its thermal dependence.
Skills for mastering experimental techniques which are widely used in solid-state materials science.

Choosing right instruments or modules for the implementation of an experimental setup in materials science, making correct interconnections between them with/or without the aid of a control computer, finding the useful range of instrument/module functionality for each specific experimental need.
Conducting experimental measurements, in-situ assessing of their reliability based on known material properties.

Assessment of the experimental results by i) verifying (or not) the expected material, ii) studying of its known properties with assessment of material quality always within the range of trust imposed by experimental error and iii) proposing ways to remedy or bypass methodology drawbacks in future attempts to run the same fabrication and/or characterization experiments, as a way to improve the quality of materials and the accuracy of the experimental results.
Analysis and synthesis of data and information, with the use of the necessary technology.
Production of free, creative and inductive thinking.

syllabus_topics: Mechanical properties of metals and polymeric materials.
Mechanical properties of solid materials under tension: elastic, inelastic and plastic deformation.
Stress-strain curves and determination of their final mechanical properties.
Determination of viscoelastic properties (bode plot).
Introduction to the fine element analysis method.
Use of finite element software to solve elasticity equations and calculate stresses, modes of displacements of components and objects.
Definition of carrier geometry, definition of materials, definition of loads, mesh generation and numerical solution of the model.
Visualization of stress concentration and gradient through photoelasticity.
Study of the stress profiles of the materials/samples under investigation with circular polarimetry.
Measurement and analytic calculation of deflections in beam bending.
Utilize an experimental apparatus to study stresses and deformations in beams under bending loads.
Doping of a semiconductor with thermal diffusion doping.
Introduction to ellipsometry: thickness measurements of the thin thermal oxide layer on silicon.
Preparation of an insulator with the Pechini method.
Dielectric materials.
Dielectric polarization and dependence of permittivity on frequency and temperatures.
Structural properties and Curie (temperature) phase transition.
Sputtering and thin-film deposition.
Townsend relation-Paschen curve.
Plasma creation.
Ion-collision stimulated sublimation of a metal target.
Need of the 'magnetron'.
Arrival of atoms, adsorption, clustering and nucleation, 2D (Frank-Van der Merwe) and 3D (Volmer-Weber) growth of thin films.
Study of the dependence of thin-film growth rate on chamber pressure and operating ion current.
Resistivity measurements (4pt probe technique) on thin metal films and dependence on the growth rate.
Electrical characterization of doped semiconductors: case study on silicon.
Ellipsometric measurement of thermal oxide thickness and chemical etching of the oxide.
Paint and fire technique for making metal contacts on silicon.
Van der Pauw measurement of conductivity.
Hall measurement of carrier type and mobility.
Acquiring a dark current-voltage curve of a silicon diode.
Measurement of ideality factor.
Structural and dielectric characterization of an insulator.
Basic principles of X-Ray diffraction on single crystals and polycrystalline materials: Bragg notation and Laue equations, crystallite size and distortion effects.
Introduction in the Lock-In amplification technique.
teaching_methods: Laboratory exercises (human-instrument interaction through a computer graphical user interface)
Access to course electronic class for announcements, lab manual, regulations, and reading material
Writing lab reports with a computer
Homework and study for the final written exam

assessment_methods.method: Evaluation of each written lab report

assessment_rules: The course grade comprises a written progress test, evaluation of each written lab report, and a final written examination. The progress test assesses knowledge of basic material properties and theoretical/practical aspects of experimental materials' characterization techniques. Lab reports are evaluated on completeness, proper processing of experimental data, accurate determination of material quantities and errors, and critical assessment of results. The final examination is based on utilizing and analyzing experimental data for problems similar to those encountered during the course.
